title: Contact Lens Red Eye: From Sterile to Sight-Threatening
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide for the diagnosis, classification, and evidence-based management of ocular surface complications associated with contact lens wear, ranging from benign mechanical issues to sight-threatening microbial keratitis.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Contact Lens-Related Red Eye (CLRRE) is a broad umbrella term encompassing various inflammatory, infectious, mechanical, and toxic conditions of the ocular surface triggered by contact lens (CL) wear. It ranges from mild, self-limiting sterile infiltrates to fulminant corneal melting. Understanding the distinction between sterile and infectious etiologies is the cornerstone of Ophthalmic management.

rows: Acute pain on waking, circumcorneal flush
Asymptomatic to mild pain, localized redness

sections.title: Microbial Keratitis (MK): The Emergency
content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Most common; rapid liquefactive necrosis and 'soupy' discharge.
Acanthamoeba: Risk factors include tap water or hot tub use; hallmark is pain out of proportion to findings.
Fungal Keratitis: Fusarium (linked to ReNu with MoistureLoc historical outbreak) or Candida.
Clinical Sign: Infiltrative focus >1.5mm, central location, and associated hypopyon.

sections.title: Clinical Examination Workflow
content: 1. Visual Acuity: Essential baseline (loss of lines suggests MK).
2. External Exam: Note discharge (purulent vs. watery) and lid edema.
3. Slit-lamp Bio-microscopy: Assess infiltrate size, depth, and location.
4. Fluorescein Staining: Check for epithelial defect (1:1 ratio with infiltrate in MK).
5. Evert Lids: Check for Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis (GPC).
6. Anterior Chamber: Look for cell/flare or hypopyon.

content.explanation: P: Pain (Severe in MK); E: Epithelial defect (Present/Large); D: Discharge (Purulent); A: Anterior chamber reaction; L: Location (Central/Axial).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Culture Required
content: Infiltrate size > 2mm in greatest diameter
Infiltrate within 2-3mm of the visual axis (Central)
Significant Anterior Chamber Reaction or Hypopyon
Rapidly progressive stromal thinning (Melting)
Atypical presentation (e.g., ring-shaped infiltrate)

sections.title: Management Protocol: Sterile Infiltrates
content: 1. Cease all Contact Lens wear immediately.
2. Rule out infection: If small, peripheral, and no staining, treat as sterile.
3. Combination Therapy: Tobradex or Maxitrol (Steroid/Antibiotic combo) QID.
4. Monitor: Review in 24 hours. Infiltrate should stabilize or improve.
5. Refit: Once resolved, consider switching to Daily Disposables or high Dk/t material.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Bacterial MK
content: 1. Culture before antibiotics if meeting Red Flag criteria.
2. Loading Dose: Fluoroquinolone (Vigamox/Zymaxid) every 15 mins for 1 hour.
3. Maintenance: Hourly drops day and night for 24-48 hours.
4. Fortified Antibiotics: For severe cases (Vancomycin 25-50mg/ml, Tobramycin 14mg/ml).
5. Cycloplegia: Atropine 1% BID to reduce ciliary spasm and synechiae.
6. Adjuvant Steroids: Consider ONLY after 48h of sterilization (SCUT study).

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Corneal Scarring: Can lead to permanent loss of BCVA if on visual axis.
Irregular Astigmatism: Resulting from stromal loss or scarring.
Perforation: Requires tectonic PK or cyanoacrylate glue.
Recurrence: High risk if CL hygiene habits do not change.
Prognosis: Excellent for sterile cases; guarded for Acanthamoeba/Fungal MK.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never 'top-off' contact lens solution; this creates a nidus for resistant biofilms.
Always culture the contact lens case and the lenses themselves if the corneal scraping is negative.
Acanthamoeba Keratitis hallmark: Radial Keratoneuritis (inflamed corneal nerves).
Solution-induced Keratopathy (SiK) often presents as diffuse punctate epithelial erosions (PEE) in a 'doughnut' pattern.
Corneal Neovascularization >2mm is a sign of chronic hypoxia and requires a lens material change.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The SCUT (Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial) showed that adjunctive topical corticosteroids do not improve visual outcomes at 3 months for most bacterial ulcers but may benefit those with central, deep, or severe ulcers. Recent developments include antimicrobial contact lenses (Silver/Selenium coated) and the use of PACK-CXL (Photoactivated Chromophore for Keratitis-Cross-linking) as an adjuvant treatment for multi-drug resistant infections.

content.explanation: Instruct patients to remove lenses if they experience: R: Redness; S: Sensitivity (to light); V: Vision changes; P: Pain.
